desc:
You are given two lists of closed intervals [start, end] with integer endpoints. Inside each list the intervals are sorted by start and pairwise disjoint: the next interval always starts strictly after the previous one ends. Intervals from different lists may overlap in any way.

Return the union of both lists as one sorted list of disjoint closed intervals. Two intervals must be merged into one when they overlap or share at least one point, for example [2, 4] and [4, 7] become [2, 7]. Intervals that merely sit next to each other without sharing a point, such as [1, 2] and [3, 4], stay separate.

firstList  = [[1, 3], [6, 9]]
secondList = [[2, 4], [5, 6], [10, 12]]
result     = [[1, 4], [5, 9], [10, 12]]
constraints: The result has no two intervals that overlap or share a point
hints: Concatenating both lists and sorting then merging works in O(n log n), but both lists are already sorted.
At every step the next interval to process is the one with the smaller start among the two list fronts, just like the merge step of merge sort.

Take the front interval with the smaller start. If its start is at most the end of the last interval in the result, extend that last interval's end to the maximum of the two ends; otherwise append it as a new interval.
editorial: Merge the two lists exactly as in merge sort: repeatedly pick the front interval with the smaller start, so the intervals are visited in order of increasing start. Combine this with the usual interval-coalescing rule: if the picked interval starts at or before the end of the last interval in the output, it touches or overlaps it, so extend the output interval's end to max(end, picked end). Otherwise it begins a new component and is appended.

Visiting intervals by increasing start guarantees that once an interval is closed off (the next start is beyond its end), nothing later can reach back to it. Each interval is visited once, so the time is O(n + m); only the output is stored.
